title: How to Pace a Demonstration and Explanation So Your Audience Can Follow Every Step
summary: By Fandi Hasib How can you help an audience keep up when you explain a process while demonstrating it? I recommend first telling everyone what to watch for in the current step, then completing an action with a clear…

body.intro:
By Fandi Hasib

How can you help an audience keep up when you explain a process while demonstrating it? I recommend first telling everyone what to watch for in the current step, then completing an action with a clear result, and finally pausing to point out what has changed. Using a simple demonstration as an example, this article explains how to coordinate speech, actions, and observation time so that both an audience in the room and viewers watching a video know which step they are seeing.

I am Fandi Hasib. My professional background includes news reporting, television news presenting, and program production in Indonesia, as well as public speaking training and BIPA, or Indonesian language education for foreign speakers. In the creator education program at PT. Otto Media Grup, my areas of focus include public speaking and content production. The company also provides opportunities for me to teach public speaking courses open to the public. Explaining a process to others requires both clear language and careful planning of what they will be able to see.
body.heading1: First, Explain What to Watch For in This Step
body.section1:
Before starting a demonstration, explain what the audience will see at the end and which step you will perform now. For example, when demonstrating a fold with a sheet of paper, you could first show the paper in its original state, then say, “For this step, watch how the two edges line up.” This example is simply an exercise in explaining a process, not an instruction on how to use a particular product.

If you begin by saying, “Watch while I do this,” the audience has to work out the object, the action, and the purpose all at once. Stating the observation goal in advance allows you to focus on showing the key point as the action takes place. Any new terms introduced during the demonstration should also be explained at the point where they become necessary for understanding.
body.heading2: After Each Action, Allow Time to Recognize the Result
body.section2:
I recommend first dividing the demonstration into short segments with visible results. Continuing with the paper example, you could show the alignment, the fold, and then the crease after unfolding the paper. Your explanation does not need to describe every tiny hand movement, but it should identify the changes the audience needs to compare.

After completing a key action, keep the object in a visible position before explaining the result. For example: “This crease now divides the sheet into two sections.” Give the audience a chance to see that change clearly before moving to the next step. Adjust the length of the pause to the content, the distance from the audience, and feedback in the room. There is no need to use the same number of seconds for every step.

If the audience is expected to follow along with their own materials, clearly distinguish between “Watch the demonstration first” and “Now it is your turn to try.” Do not continue explaining essential conditions for the next step while they are looking for materials. Check their progress at an appropriate point before deciding whether to continue.

Replace “Look Here” with Specific Descriptions

Phrases such as “Press this,” “Move it here,” and “Now it is done” are difficult to understand on their own without the visuals. Instead, name the object, its position, and the change involved. For example: “Move the top edge to the bottom edge so that the two edges line up.” Also clarify whether directions refer to the view seen by the audience or the perspective of the person performing the demonstration, and avoid switching back and forth.

Guidance from W3C on describing visual information explains that visual descriptions essential to understanding a video can be incorporated naturally into the script. When preparing an instructional demonstration, I recommend using this principle to check whether your words provide the information needed to understand a step if the audience cannot see a particular detail clearly.

Descriptions should focus on meaningful changes. There is no need to read out everything in the background. When assessing a result, explain the basis for that assessment wherever possible. For example, say, “The edges are now aligned,” rather than simply, “That is correct.” This helps the audience understand what to look for instead of merely accepting your conclusion.

Check the Demonstration from the Audience Perspective First

Before giving the explanation, check the actual venue to see whether the object is too small, whether your hands block a key area, and whether you can still be heard clearly while demonstrating. When presenting to a camera, review the actual framing as well to check whether any key action falls outside the shot. Adjust your position and the demonstration angle to improve visibility, rather than aiming for larger movements.

When a demonstration involves on-screen operations, moving the mouse alone may not make the intended target clear. First name the area you intend to open, then perform the action and describe the actual change on the screen. If the interface or result differs from what you expected, stop and check. Do not continue reciting your prepared explanation while the audience is looking at a different screen.

Use a Short Recording to Check That Speech and Visuals Match

Choose a demonstration segment of approximately ninety seconds, record it, and review it in two separate passes. First, watch the visuals to confirm that the observation goal and the results of the actions are visible. Then listen to the audio to check whether the objects, sequence, and key changes are clearly explained. The ninety-second length and two-pass review are practical arrangements for rehearsal, not course standards or measures of effectiveness.

Finally, review the audio and visuals together. If you say, “It is complete,” while the action is still in progress on screen, adjust your wording or pause. If the action has already moved to the next step while the audio is still explaining the previous stage, revise their sequence. The goal is to help the audience connect the current sentence with the current action.

Creator education at PT. Otto Media Grup connects public speaking with content production. For recordings of classes open to the public, live demonstrations, and branded content in Media Tech settings, clear explanations need to be prepared alongside filming arrangements. Equipment can record the process, but the speaker is responsible for clearly explaining its purpose, changes, and the basis for assessing results.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should You Keep Talking Throughout a Demonstration?

No. Key actions can be accompanied by brief explanations, and pauses can give the audience time to observe the results. Continuous talking does not mean you are continuously providing useful information.

Should You Start Again from the Beginning if the Audience Cannot Keep Up?

First, identify the step where they lost track. If a particular action was unclear, return to that step and show it from a different angle. If they did not understand a prerequisite, explain the necessary background.

What Should You Do if a Live Demonstration Does Not Produce the Expected Result?

First, describe what has actually happened and pause before proceeding further. Explain the cause only when you can do so accurately. If you cannot confirm it at that moment, do not invent an explanation on the spot. You can instead use a clearly labeled example prepared in advance.

If a Video Has Captions, Do You Still Need to Describe the Visuals Verbally?

Captions primarily convey speech and other audio information. They do not automatically supply visual details that have not been spoken aloud. Actions and changes necessary for understanding the content should still be provided through appropriate descriptions or other accessible formats.

Closing Thoughts

The next time you prepare a demonstration, I recommend selecting the step that the audience most needs to understand visually, then practicing the observation goal, action, and explanation of the result together. When your words direct attention to the visuals and your actions allow time for observation, the audience can more easily follow the process and understand your explanation.

title: How to Write Speech Cue Cards That Help You Regain Your Train of Thought When You Forget What to Say
summary: By Fandi Hasib Worried about forgetting what to say during a speech? What should you put on your cue cards? I recommend making each card a roadmap you can navigate at a glance: what this section needs to explain, which…

body.intro:
By Fandi Hasib

Worried about forgetting what to say during a speech? What should you put on your cue cards? I recommend making each card a roadmap you can navigate at a glance: what this section needs to explain, which example to use, and where to go next. Clearly mark any material that must be quoted accurately in a separate place. Through sample cards and rehearsal methods, this article explains how to recover your train of thought when you briefly get stuck, rather than looking down to search for an entire passage in your script.

News reporting requires accuracy, and public speaking also requires clear communication with the audience. I am Fandi Hasib. I have worked as a journalist, television news anchor, and program producer in Indonesia, as well as in public speaking training and BIPA, or Indonesian language teaching for foreign speakers. I participate in creator education programs at PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content production, and teach public speaking classes open to the public through opportunities provided by the company. When preparing a speech, I recommend first distinguishing between material that must be delivered word for word and material that can be expressed naturally around its intended meaning.
body.heading1: First, Decide What Your Cue Cards Need to Do
body.section1:
Cue cards can help you keep track of the sequence or remind you of conditions that are easy to overlook. They do not necessarily need to contain the full speech. If an event requires you to read a formal statement, or if there is source material that must be quoted accurately, prepare the corresponding full text. There is no need to force it into keywords simply to appear more practiced.

For a general knowledge-sharing talk, start by writing one sentence that states the purpose of each section, such as “Explain why the audience should be identified first.” Then choose prompts that bring specific content to mind. Words such as “key point” and “example” are too broad; “beginners versus people familiar with the process” makes it easier to recall the comparison you intended to make. Ultimately, you need to rehearse with the cards yourself to determine whether they work.

In a practice article about reducing reliance on a script, Toastmasters International describes gradually condensing notes into keywords. The principle worth borrowing here is to use keywords to prompt your train of thought; the number of cards and the amount of text should be adjusted to suit the content, reading needs, and setting.
body.heading2: Keep Navigation Cues in Consistent Positions
body.section2:
Take a short talk about preparing for a recording as an example. You could reserve the top of the card for the section title, place specific prompts in the middle, and use the bottom to indicate how to transition to the next section. The following is a layout devised for illustration. It is neither a standard template nor an example from an actual class.

Card numbers help you recover the sequence, while section titles help you recover the meaning. If you write only a number without a content prompt, you may still be unsure what to say next when you lose your place. If a piece of information must be stated in full, such as an applicable condition or the source of a quotation, write it clearly on a separate line. Do not condense it so much that its original meaning is lost.

Readability Matters More Than Fitting Everything In

I recommend checking the cards at the distance and under the lighting conditions in which you will actually use them. If you need to bring them closer to read them clearly, reduce the content or increase the text size. Do not make the text tiny just to keep everything on a single card. Paper size, font size, and contrast should all support your own reading needs.

Paper cards can be used on one side only and arranged in sequence to reduce shuffling. For electronic prompts, test how to move between pages and whether the screen turns off automatically. If the setting permits, prepare a backup outline that you can consult at any time. The priority is reliable access to your prompts, not a preference for any particular device.

When You Get Stuck, First Recover the Meaning of the Section

If you suddenly forget the original wording, pause briefly, look at the section title on the card, and establish how much you have already explained. If you have covered the core information, use a natural transition to move into the next section. If you have omitted a condition that affects understanding, clarify it before continuing.

For example, if the card says “Explain differences between audiences,” you could restate the point: “The distinction we need to make here is whether the audience is already familiar with the basic process.” This is a practice sentence for resuming the talk, not a fixed line to memorize. Its purpose is to bring both you and the audience back to the current topic, rather than restart the entire speech.

If you forget a specific number, name, or quotation, do not fill the gap with something that merely sounds close. Consult the accurate notes you have prepared. If you cannot verify the information at that moment, clearly state that it needs to be checked, rather than presenting a guess as fact. Cue cards should support accurate communication, not serve as a reason to fill in information arbitrarily.

Use Three Short Practice Runs to Check Whether the Cards Work

Choose the same short passage for three practice runs. In the first, deliver it in the normal sequence. In the second, start from a section in the middle to check whether you can find your place. In the third, glance at a prompt during a natural pause, then continue speaking. Three runs are simply a practice plan, not a threshold for proficiency.

After each run, note only what did not work well on the card: were the prompts too abstract, was the text too crowded, or was the transition unclear? Revise the relevant part, then try again. Focus your assessment on whether you omitted any essential conditions and whether you resumed the content smoothly. There is no need to use exactly the same wording every time.

In creator education at PT. Otto Media Grup, preparing prompts can also support classes open to the public, on-camera presentations, and live-streamed explanations. Media Tech tools can hold scripts and prompts, but speakers still need to test them personally to confirm that the content is easy to locate, clear to read, and easy to resume during actual delivery.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Using Cue Cards Look Unprofessional?

Professionalism cannot be judged solely by whether someone uses cards. What matters more is whether the information is accurate, the explanation is clear, and checking the prompts interrupts communication. When necessary, you can take a natural glance at a card and continue.

What Is the Maximum Number of Words You Can Put on a Card?

There is no fixed word count that works for everyone. Test the card at your actual reading distance. If you need to keep looking down and searching, you should usually reduce the content or divide it into smaller sections.

Do You Need to Memorize the Entire Speech?

Word-for-word memorization does not need to be the goal for every speech. First, become familiar with the content structure and key facts. When material must be read out accurately, keeping the full text is more appropriate.

Can You Skip a Section After Forgetting What to Say?

First, determine whether skipping it would affect what follows. If it contains an essential definition, step, or limiting condition, briefly supply the missing information. If it is merely an optional supporting example, you can omit it as long as doing so does not disrupt the logic.

Closing Thoughts

I recommend taking a passage from an existing script and first creating a card that identifies its purpose, specific prompts, and the next step. Then use it in a rehearsal. A good cue card does not need to supply every sentence for you. It needs to help you find the meaning you genuinely want to convey next when you pause.

title: How to Cut a Lecture Recording into Short Videos: Preserve the Context That Makes the Point Hold
summary: To cut a lecture into short videos, you can first select an independent question, then preserve the background, conditions, and explanations necessary to answer that question. The length of a clip should be determined by…

body.intro:
To cut a lecture into short videos, you can first select an independent question, then preserve the background, conditions, and explanations necessary to answer that question. The length of a clip should be determined by whether the meaning is complete, and the title must not be more absolute than the original words. This article explains, from segment selection and subtitles to pre-publication checks, how to enable people who have not watched the full lecture to accurately understand the content.

A passage may sound clear in the live setting but become confusing when placed alone in a short video. The audience knows what was asked earlier; those who scroll onto the clip may not. Creators therefore need to accommodate two viewing conditions at once: the original full-length explanation, and the clip that appears independently after leaving the original setting.

The professional background of Fandi Hasib spans both of these settings. He has worked in Indonesian news reporting, television news anchoring and program production, as well as public speaking training and BIPA Indonesian language education. Currently, he participates in the creator education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content production, and has been given the opportunity by the company to teach public open classes on public speaking. Considering expression and production together also provides a concrete entry point for discussing the editing of lecture recordings.
body.heading1: First Find a Question That Can Be Answered Independently
body.section1:
When selecting a clip, you can first write down a single audience question for it, for example, "When introducing a new product, what should the first sentence say." Then return to the recording and look for the passage that actually answers this question. A raised voice, applause from the audience, or a single sentence that sounds impactful is not sufficient on its own to prove that this segment is suitable for independent publication.

Suppose there is a twelve-minute sharing session, and a production exercise hopes to select two clips from it. These two are merely an example, not a platform requirement or output metric. First confirm separately what question each segment answers; if both segments depend on the same background, you can supplement the necessary explanation, or reselect one of them—there is no need to make up the number.
body.heading2: Do Not Start Cutting Directly from a Powerful Sentence
body.section2:
Suppose the original statement was: "If the audience already understands the basic steps, you can shorten the background introduction and leave the time for the demonstration." Keeping only "you can shorten the background introduction" removes the condition under which this suggestion applies. Although the clipped content comes from the same sentence, its meaning has become broader. This self-constructed example shows that checking accuracy cannot rely solely on whether every word comes from the original recording.

Attention should also be paid to references such as "this matter," "the second situation," and "the earlier example." They have clear referents in the live setting but may lose their referents once placed in a standalone clip. One option is to retain the preceding sentence, or to add concise and accurate contextual notes on screen; the added text should let the audience recognize that it is an editorial note and must not masquerade as words actually spoken by the speaker.

Using a Checklist to Review What Was Cut

The table below is intended for item-by-item review of editing decisions, not as a scoring scale for rating the video. Whenever a cut would change the scope of applicability of a viewpoint, one should return to the original recording to reconfirm.

Subject Subtitles and Titles to the Same Check

Auto-generated subtitles can serve as a starting point for editing, but sentence-by-sentence verification is still required before publishing. Pay particular attention to names of people, names of institutions, numbers, and negations. For example, dropping "not recommended to copy directly" into "recommended to copy directly" reverses the recommendation even if the visuals are unchanged. Subtitle proofreading should be based on the original audio and clear context.

Titles must also return to the same question. If the speaker is discussing "methods worth trying for a first recording," the title should not be written as "all creators must do this." A title can be more concise than spoken expression, but it should retain the objects and constraints that affect understanding. If a short title cannot accommodate these conditions, use a different phrasing rather than quietly deleting the conditions.

When choosing cover images, also consider whether facial expressions and accompanying graphics lead the audience to form judgments not present in the original segment. Images used to illustrate steps should not be staged as proof of results, and illustrative graphics should not mislead viewers into thinking they are records of real projects.

Leave a Path Back to the Original Recording for Each Segment

Internally, the team can record for each segment the original file name, start and end times, and the corresponding question. For example, "sample recording 03:20 to 04:15, explaining when to shorten the background introduction" is merely an example of the record format. This way, when checking subtitles or adjusting titles, editors can return to the original segment instead of judging solely on the basis of an already shortened file.

In the release notes, a source link may be provided when accessible original content genuinely exists; when there is no public full version, do not fabricate a link or write it as if the full version can be watched. Key conditions that viewers need to understand should be kept directly in the short video and cannot be left entirely to another link to carry.

The creator education of PT. Otto Media Grup connects public speaking with content production. Placed in the context of Media Tech and brand-creator collaboration, segment records, subtitle checking, and version management can serve as concrete working suggestions: the technical side is responsible for helping organize materials, and the editor is responsible for judging whether the content still holds after leaving its original context. Putting these checks into daily production gives the team a clear basis for verification when revising the same piece of material.

Frequently Asked Questions

How Long Is the Most Suitable Length for a Short Video

First look at whether a question can be answered completely, then check the requirements according to the actual publishing channel. This article does not set a uniform duration, nor does it treat any particular number of seconds as a guarantee of dissemination effect.

Can Sentences from Different Positions Be Spliced Together

Merging content on the same topic can be considered, but it should be checked whether the splicing changes temporal relations, conditions, or positions. If it is easily understood as continuous original speech, clear editing or explanatory methods should be adopted.

Can Adding One Subtitle Restore All the Context

No. When the context is complex or there are too many qualifying conditions, subtitles may not be clear enough. You can keep a more complete clip, split it into a standalone explanation, or abandon this selection.

What Is the Single Most Worthwhile Check Before Publishing

Ask someone who has not seen the original talk to watch the final cut first, state the points they understood and the intended audience, then compare with the original segment. This helps identify comprehension gaps, but it cannot replace editorial verification.

Conclusion

The key to shortening a talk lies in ensuring the point can still be accurately understood after leaving the venue. The next time you select a segment, first write out the question it is meant to answer, then check whether the removed parts contain the conditions that make the answer valid. Preserve these conditions, and the clip has a foundation for standalone publication.

title: How to Close the Final Minute of a Speech So the Audience Leaves with a Clear Conclusion
summary: Author Fandi Hasib When a speech reaches its end, how do you close it naturally and clearly? I suggest returning to the problem raised at the opening, stating the conclusion in one sentence, and then giving the audience…

body.intro:
Author Fandi Hasib

When a speech reaches its end, how do you close it naturally and clearly? I suggest returning to the problem raised at the opening, stating the conclusion in one sentence, and then giving the audience a next step commensurate with the content. Do not open a new topic at the end. This article uses self-devised examples and a one-minute rehearsal to explain how to connect the summary, the call to action, and the closing remarks, so that the audience knows what this sharing session has actually left them with.

I am Fandi Hasib. I have worked in Indonesia as a journalist, television news anchor, and program producer, and I also work in public speaking training and BIPA Indonesian language education. I participate in the creator education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, focusing on public speaking and content production, and the company also provides me with opportunities to teach public classes on public speaking. When preparing a sharing session, I suggest writing the final few sentences down separately, because they carry the task of drawing the entire content together.
body.heading1: The Summary Should Answer the Question, Not Recite the Agenda
body.section1:
If the opening raised "what should I prepare first for a first voice-over recording," then ending with "today we covered preparation, shooting, and checking" is merely reviewing the sequence. It could be changed to: "For a first voice-over recording, you can first get one question across completely, then check the sound and the picture." This sentence still needs to be supported by the preceding content and cannot suddenly become a different judgment at the end. Both formulations here are practice examples.

I suggest reading the opening question and the closing conclusion together. Do they correspond? If what was discussed earlier is a method suitable for beginners, then at the end do not present it as the only method for everyone. The necessary subjects and conditions should also be retained at the end.

The speech writing and delivery guide of Toastmasters International also suggests emphasizing the main point in the conclusion and proposing a call to action accordingly. Applied to a specific speech, the next step should match the actual needs of the audience and does not have to become a registration or purchase request every time.
body.heading2: Write the Next Step as an Action the Audience Can Begin
body.section2:
"I hope everyone will improve their communication skills" expresses a wish, but does not tell the audience where to start. It can be written as a small action, for example: "Before the next recording, first write down in one sentence the question this piece of content is meant to answer." This suggestion does not require the audience to complete a full training program on the spot, nor does it promise any particular degree of improvement.

A single ending can retain just one primary action. If the audience is asked to simultaneously bookmark, follow, fill out a form, download materials, and sign up, the priorities need to be reorganized. State first the one item most relevant to this content, and when there is indeed supplementary information, arrange it on a resource page or in a follow-up note.

Some speeches aim at understanding and do not need to arrange external actions. For example, when explaining the difference between two content formats, the audience can be asked to look at an example again using the judgment criteria just given. The ending can also leave a bounded thinking question, rather than forcing in a call to action.

Rehearse with One Minute, but Do Not Treat the Seconds as a Formula

Sixty seconds can be set aside for one practice run: the first twenty seconds return to the topic and summarize the conclusion, the middle twenty-five seconds explain one action worth trying, and the final fifteen seconds set out the closing or Q&A arrangements. This is merely a time allocation convenient for rehearsal, not a research finding, nor a standard applicable to all speeches.

If the summary takes a long time to state clearly, first check whether the body is simultaneously carrying too many objectives. If the action invitation can only be read out in a rush, cut the side explanations beyond the supplementary conditions. Do not suddenly speed up to catch up with the seconds, and there is no need to add a new point just to fill the time.

During practice, the ending can be recorded after the final paragraph of the body. A sentence that reads smoothly on its own may, when placed back into the full text, repeat something already said. Listen to the whole segment, then decide which information needs to be kept and which was left to the end only because of a reluctance to cut it.

After the Q&A Ends, Bring the Thread Back

If a Q&A session is arranged after the sharing, you can first give a brief summary, then clearly tell the audience that the Q&A is beginning. When the Q&A ends, use one sentence to connect back to the main theme of the talk. The last question may only concern a specific detail; there is no need to let that detail automatically become the final conclusion of the entire sharing.

The closing remarks also need to suit the on-site arrangements. You can thank the audience, then hand over to the host, or explain the next segment. After speaking, stop naturally and do not follow up with "one more thing." Content that is truly important but cannot be covered in time can be left for appropriate follow-up communication.

For the creator education involved with PT. Otto Media Grup, this kind of closing practice can connect public classes, livestreams, and content production. The technical tools in the Media Tech scenario can help with recording and distribution, but speakers still need to judge for themselves: whether the conclusion left at the end is accurate, and whether the action the audience is invited to take is clear.

Frequently Asked Questions

Must the Ending Use a Punchy One-Liner?

No. Accurately answering the core question is more important than pursuing a beautiful sentence. Even with a short and powerful expression, the conditions that determine the meaning cannot be omitted.

Can I Just Say "Thank You All"?

Acknowledgements can be kept, but it is best to complete the necessary summary first. Acknowledgements are responsible for closing politely, while the conclusion is responsible for stating the main point the audience should take away.

What Do I Do If I Suddenly Realize I Left Something Out

First determine whether it would change conclusions already stated. Necessary corrections should be stated immediately; additions that do not affect the conclusion can be left for Q&A or follow-up materials, and there is no need to restart the entire presentation.

How to Judge Whether There Are Too Many Calls to Action

Try having a practice partner listen only to the ending, and then state the main next step. If the person lists many unrelated tasks, priorities need to be re-established. This feedback is used for revising the draft and does not represent actual conversion results.

Conclusion

The next time you prepare a presentation, I suggest first writing the one sentence you want to leave behind, and then checking whether the body can support it. Let the summary have an answer, let the next step be able to begin, and then end naturally. A clear ending can start with one serious trial run.

title: How Gestures and Staging Work Together in a Speech: Move With Purpose
summary: Author: Fandi Hasib When giving a speech, if you do not know where to put your hands, or you always want to pace back and forth, I suggest first clarifying what the audience needs to pay attention to in the current…

body.intro:
Author: Fandi Hasib

When giving a speech, if you do not know where to put your hands, or you always want to pace back and forth, I suggest first clarifying what the audience needs to pay attention to in the current sentence, and then choosing a movement that supports the meaning. When no movement is necessary, you can naturally pause. This article starts with gestures, staging, and camera framing, and offers practice methods that you can adjust yourself, to help speakers prepare bodily expression together with content.

My experience includes work as an Indonesian journalist, television news anchor, and program producer, as well as public speaking training and BIPA Indonesian language education. I am Fandi Hasib, currently involved in the creator education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, focusing on public speaking and content production, and I have been given the opportunity by the company to teach a public speaking open course. When facing a stage or a camera, I suggest choosing an expression approach based on the actual space, equipment, and personal physical conditions, rather than imitating a uniform movement template.
body.heading1: First Give the Hands a Natural Starting Point
body.section1:
At the start of a trial presentation, you can let your hands rest in a position that is comfortable for you, and then observe whether movement is needed when you get to specific content. Holding a cue card or a remote control does not mean the other hand must keep moving. The key point is to avoid having your attention pulled away from the content you are explaining because you are constantly thinking about "what to do with my hands."

I do not suggest treating any particular hand posture as proof of confidence or its absence. Posture is affected by habit, venue, equipment, and physical conditions. A more useful question during practice is: does the movement block the object being demonstrated, does it conflict with the current meaning, and can you comfortably complete the explanation.
body.heading2: Let Gestures Correspond to Specific Relationships
body.section2:
When explaining size, position, order, or two options, you can try using hand gestures to help present the relationships. For example, when comparing two proposals, you can leave a position on each side of your body; when returning to the same proposal later, still use the corresponding position. This approach is only a practice example and needs to be adjusted according to the audience perspective and on-site conditions.

When listing steps, you can coordinate finger counting with the number, but you do not need to pair every sentence with a gesture. If you say "two reasons" verbally while your gestures keep changing, the audience may find it hard to judge what you are emphasizing. You can first finish the whole sentence, then review whether the gestures are consistent with the expression. Important meanings must still be stated clearly in language and cannot rely solely on movements for conveyance.

Place Movement At Content Transitions

In a space that allows movement, you can first choose a position suitable for opening and delivering key points. Move only when you genuinely need to walk toward a demonstration object or transition from one content section to another; once you arrive, stand firm and continue explaining. There is no need to keep walking back and forth to cover the entire stage.

During practice, you can try using two positions: one for raising questions and one for explaining proposals. This is a self-defined spatial cue, not a stage rule that must be followed. If the venue is small, a fixed microphone is used, or you personally find it inconvenient to move, staying in place can equally convey structure through verbal transitions, voice, and appropriate gestures.

Before the formal start, you should also clearly check the audience sightlines, projection range, and equipment positions. Your standing position should not block the content that needs to be shown; before preparing to walk somewhere, also confirm whether you can be heard clearly there. Spatial conditions affect the choice of movements; confirm the conditions first, then decide on the arrangement.

Check Camera Movements Back In The Frame

Gestures suitable for live settings do not necessarily appear fully within the video frame. I suggest recording a short segment under the actual composition, then checking whether the hands frequently go out of frame or block the face or demonstration objects. When operations need to be shown, adjust the frame range together with the explanation arrangement, and do not rely solely on making larger movements to solve visibility issues.

In the creator education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, public speaking and content production are interconnected. For open class recording, filming, and brand content output in livestream scenarios, on-camera expression needs to account for both the live audience and the audience watching the footage. What the frame can see should become part of the trial lecture check.

Compare One Specific Change Using Two Recordings

You can first record a segment of the original explanation, then change only one arrangement, for example reducing aimless walking, or keeping the gestures for comparing two options consistent. Using the same content and a similar camera range for both segments makes it easier to observe this one change. The two recordings here are a practice setup, not a method for measuring effects.

When reviewing, listen to the audio first to confirm whether the meaning is complete, then check whether the movements help mark key points. If a movement seems deliberate, you can reduce its amplitude, reduce its frequency, or drop the movement. Do not require yourself to copy a certain posture just because others commonly use it; expression should suit the content and also suit the speaker.

Common Questions

Will Standing in One Position the Whole Time Look Stiff

Not necessarily. As long as the explanation is clear, you are comfortable, and you can pay attention to the audience, a fixed stance can also deliver effective expression; walking around does not have to be treated as a necessary condition.

How to Gesture When Holding a Microphone

First ensure the voice is stable, then use the free hand to make moderate gestures. When a two-handed demonstration is needed, appropriate equipment or a presentation method should be arranged in advance.

Can These Methods Also Be Used When Sharing While Seated

Yes. Adjust gestures according to the seat, desktop, and camera range, keep yourself comfortable, and avoid letting movements block the content that needs to be shown.

How to Know Whether a Certain Movement Should Be Kept

Check it against the current expression. If it helps present a relationship, indicate an object, or signal a transition, it can be kept; when its function cannot be explained, it can first be removed and then compared.

Conclusion

In the next rehearsal, I suggest choosing only one movement or staging issue to adjust. Let every movement and gesture have a clear expressive reason, and also allow yourself to quietly finish saying an important sentence.

title: How to Write to Speak That Listeners Can Understand
summary: Author: Fandi Hasib Why does a draft that looks complete become so laborious when spoken aloud? I suggest first reading the draft aloud, identifying sentences that require repeated re-reading to understand, then filling…

body.intro:
Author: Fandi Hasib

Why does a draft that looks complete become so laborious when spoken aloud? I suggest first reading the draft aloud, identifying sentences that require repeated re-reading to understand, then filling in missing subjects, breaking up excessive information, and retaining necessary conditions. A spoken script must help listeners follow the content through sound. This article uses rewriting examples to show how to make expression more fluent without changing the original meaning.

For me, preparing a speech script requires considering both informational accuracy and listener comprehension. I am Fandi Hasib, and I have worked in news reporting, television news broadcasting, and program production in Indonesia, as well as in public speaking training and BIPA Indonesian language teaching. I participate in the creator education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content production, and the company also provides me with opportunities to publicly teach public speaking courses. The speaking methods described below can be applied to open classes, speeches, and voiceover preparation.
body.heading1: First, Listen to Your Own Draft Once
body.section1:
Before revising, you can record a short segment and listen only to the recording without looking at the text. Note the places that make you want to stop and re-listen: is it that the sentence contains too many parallel items, or that "it" or "this point" has an unclear referent? Mark these locations, then return to the draft to address them. Do not only check whether you misread any words; also ask whether listeners can tell who is doing what.

I suggest selecting approximately two hundred characters as practice material first. This word count is merely a scope convenient for focused revision, not a standard for voiceover length. For initial practice, you do not need to rewrite the entire piece; improving one paragraph well and then checking whether adjacent paragraphs connect naturally will make it easier to see the changes brought by revision.
body.heading2: Let Actions and Subjects Appear Early
body.section2:
"Regarding the conduct of content quality assessment work" can be changed to "We will first check content quality." The latter puts the action up front, making it easier for the audience to know what to do next. But if it is unclear who exactly "we" refers to, the responsible person or team should be named; responsibility must not be blurred for the sake of brevity.

When sentences need to be split, first find the boundaries of meaning. If a sentence simultaneously introduces background, explains reasons, and assigns tasks, it can be separated; conditions that depend on each other should stay close to the conclusion. Below are self-composed sentences for practice; they do not correspond to any real project notice.

After rewriting, go back and check: who is responsible, when it should be done, what conditions must be met — has any of this been deleted? In particular, words such as "may," "only applies to," and "under certain circumstances" often limit the scope of a conclusion. Making sentences flow smoothly should not turn a conditional judgment into an unconditional promise.

Give Listeners Audible Connections

In writing, structure can be shown through headings, paragraphs, and tables, but in oral presentation the relationships also need to be stated aloud. For example, when moving from a problem to a solution, one can say, "Now that we know where the problem lies, let us look at how to adjust." When moving from one approach to another, the basis for comparison should be stated so that the audience knows why the topic is changing.

Connective phrases do not need to be the same in every paragraph. When explaining causes, make the causal relationship clear; when describing operations, state the sequence; when switching examples, explain what the example is meant to illustrate. If deleting a connective phrase loses no relationship, it can also be removed, to avoid filling the script with "next," "then," and "in summary."

Terms Can Be Retained, Explanations Should Be Placed Nearby

Professional expression does not mean using as many abstract words as possible. I suggest that when a term appears for the first time, a concrete explanation immediately follows. For example, when discussing "content review," one can explain that it means going back over published content to check the original goals, actual performance, and areas needing adjustment. The scope of the explanation should match the current topic; there is no need to unfold an entire course for a single term.

In cross-language or cross-cultural settings, one should check even more carefully whether abbreviations and industry terms need to be spelled out. Rather than assuming the audience is familiar with the same expression, it is better to add a definition at key points. When rewriting for different audiences, core facts should remain consistent, while examples and depth of explanation can be adjusted.

Connecting the Revised Draft Back to the Trial Delivery

After completing revisions, record again at a natural speaking pace. You can ask a practice partner to listen to the audio only, restate the main points, and point out places that need further explanation. Such restatement is used to identify expression problems; it does not amount to proof that all real audiences will understand. If the partner misunderstands something, first return to the relevant sentence and check references, conditions, and the order of content.

This is also a common preparatory step for public speaking and content production. Creator education at PT. Otto Media Grup involves both of these fields; in the course, livestream, and video production scenarios of Media Tech, when the same topic enters different formats, it is necessary to re-examine whether the language is suitable for being heard. Written materials can provide the basis, but the final script still needs to go through an out-loud trial delivery.

Frequently Asked Questions

Must Every Sentence Be Short

Not necessarily. Sentence length should serve completeness of meaning. The key is to make the subject, the action, and the necessary conditions clear, rather than splitting every sentence into fragments.

Can a Spoken Script Repeat Keywords

You may repeat key names at important transitions or summaries to help listeners orient themselves; there is no need to constantly swap in words with not-quite-identical meanings just to avoid repetition.

Do All Pauses Need to Be Marked on the Script

You can first mark the places where liaison easily changes meaning, as well as important transitions. The markings should be convenient for your own use; there is no need to turn the script into dense action instructions.

Can It Be Handled Solely by Automatic Rewriting Tools

Tools can help propose versions, but the speaker still needs to verify facts, conditions, and tone, and read it aloud personally. Fluent generated sentences do not automatically mean the meaning is accurate.

Conclusion

I recommend starting from a draft that is already written, reading it aloud, identifying the difficult spots, rewriting, and then listening again. By applying these checks to specific sentences, the script gets closer to an explanation that the audience can follow.

title: How to Write a Clear Brand Brief So Creators Can Start Production
summary: By the Editorial Team How can a collaboration brief help a creator understand where to begin? Start by explaining whom the content should help and what problem it should address, then distinguish information that must be…

body.intro:
By the Editorial Team

How can a collaboration brief help a creator understand where to begin? Start by explaining whom the content should help and what problem it should address, then distinguish information that must be accurate from elements that allow creative freedom. Finally, agree on deliverables and approval checkpoints. Beginning with the preparation of a short video, this article explains how to turn expectations such as “a polished feel” or “something more natural” into requirements that both sides can discuss and review.

This is also a foundational skill worth addressing in creator education. Fandi Hasib has worked as a journalist, television news anchor, and producer in Indonesia, as well as in public speaking training and BIPA Indonesian language teaching. He participates in creator education initiatives at PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content production. The company also provides opportunities for him to teach public speaking classes open to the public. These professional fields share a common question: can the person receiving the information understand it and take the next step?
body.heading1: Start With the Audience Question, Then the Brand Message
body.section1:
A collaboration brief can be understood as a set of instructions for a production assignment. When drafting one, start by completing this sentence: “After watching this content, the audience should be able to…” If the answer is “understand that the brand is great,” it is not specific enough. Change it to “understand when this feature is useful and how to start using it,” and the creator has a content task they can build around.

For example, suppose the assignment is to produce a short video introducing an audio recording tool. The audience question could be: “How can I tell whether my current environment is suitable for recording a spoken presentation at home?” Brand information should be organized around that question, rather than squeezing every selling point into the script one after another. This example simply illustrates how to define a task; it does not refer to an actual client or product.
body.heading2: Separate Factual Requirements From Creative Freedom
body.section2:
The party supplying the information needs to provide an accurate basis for product names, the scope of features, conditions of use, and demonstration steps. Creators can adapt the story angle, language style, or shot structure, but they should not broaden factual claims simply to make the content flow more smoothly. Any unverified information should remain an open question until it has been confirmed, before a decision is made on whether to include it in the script.

At the same time, specify where creators are welcome to propose ideas. For example, the core feature must be explained clearly, while the creator can design the opening to suit the audience. This preserves individual creative expression while helping both sides understand which changes require further approval. The table below provides examples of rewritten brief requirements, not project performance data.

Confirm Choices While They Are Still Easy to Change, Then Begin Filming

Confirming the topic, outline, and key visuals before filming allows both sides to identify differences in understanding earlier. For example, if one side expects a practical demonstration while the other is preparing an interview, that difference should be resolved at the outline stage. Do not wait until filming is complete to reject the content format with a vague comment such as “it does not feel right.”

One practical approach is to set two approval checkpoints: first confirm the content direction, then confirm the script and essential facts before filming. These two checkpoints are simply an example of a collaborative process; the actual workflow should reflect the complexity of the project. Each approval should leave a clearly identified version, noting which suggestions have been incorporated and which questions remain unresolved.

Feedback should also point to specific parts of the content. “The opening is a little weak” can be clarified as “the audience still does not know what problem this video addresses.” “Make this part more professional” can become “add the conditions under which this feature can be used.” This gives the creator actionable revision tasks and makes it easier for both sides to judge whether the changes address the issue.

Review the Finished Content Against Observable Delivery Requirements

Before finalizing the content, review it against the brief: whether all agreed content is included, key names are accurate, the relevant parts of the demonstration are clearly visible, the audio is clear enough to understand, and the files meet the approved specifications. Views, comments, and inquiries are results to observe after publication. They cannot replace a pre-delivery content review, nor should they be casually guaranteed in the brief.

These collaboration skills connect naturally with creator education at PT. Otto Media Grup. Across Media Tech, digital marketing, MCNs, and brand–creator collaborations, a brief can help content planning, on-camera delivery, and production execution stay focused on the same goal. It provides a shared basis for discussion, while actual effectiveness still needs to be assessed through records from real projects.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a More Detailed Brief Always Better?

The level of detail should be sufficient to support production. Clearly state the facts that must be accurate, the required visuals, and the delivery requirements, while leaving reasonable room for creative expression.

Can We Just Send a Reference Video?

A reference video can support communication, but explain exactly what should be used as a reference, such as the order of explanation, camera distance, or demonstration method. This helps prevent each side from interpreting it differently.

Can We Use a Different Opening Proposed by the Creator?

Discuss it in relation to the audience task and factual boundaries. As long as the new opening serves the objective and does not change information that must remain accurate, there is room to compare approaches and rehearse the delivery.

How Should New Requirements During Filming Be Handled?

First explain how the additional requirements affect the content, production arrangements, and scope of delivery. Then jointly approve an updated version, rather than treating requirements that have not been discussed as part of the original assignment.

Closing Thoughts

A useful content brief should tell creators whom they are helping, what they need to explain clearly, and what needs to be confirmed next. Before your next collaboration, start by turning the vaguest requirement into a specific statement that can be discussed. Then ask the other person to restate the task in their own words, and use that as the starting point for refining the brief.

title: How to Make Smooth Handoffs in a Two-Person Presentation and Keep the Audience on Track
summary: When two people present together, how can they avoid repeating explanations, switching speakers abruptly, or speaking at the same time? I recommend dividing responsibilities according to the questions the audience needs…

body.intro:
Author: Fandi Hasib

When two people present together, how can they avoid repeating explanations, switching speakers abruptly, or speaking at the same time? I recommend dividing responsibilities according to the questions the audience needs answered, then agreeing on transition phrases, ways to pick up from each other, and cues to use during the presentation. Every change of speaker should make two things clear to the audience: what has just been explained and why the other person is taking over next. This article uses sample dialogue and a short rehearsal exercise to help presenting partners bring their separately prepared material together into one cohesive presentation.

I am Fandi Hasib. My professional background includes news reporting, television news presenting, and program production in Indonesia, as well as public speaking training and BIPA Indonesian language education for foreign learners. I currently participate in creator education initiatives at PT. Otto Media Grup, focusing on public speaking and content production. The company also provides opportunities for me to teach public speaking classes open to the public. For co-hosting or joint presentations, I recommend preparing the transitions between speakers as a distinct part of the process.
body.heading1: Divide Responsibilities Around Audience Questions
body.section1:
During preparation, start by writing down the questions the presentation should help the audience answer, then decide who will cover each section. Suppose two creators are jointly introducing preparations for a video shoot: one explains how to choose a suitable environment for recording sound, while the other demonstrates how to check the recording. Their responsibilities differ, but both work toward the same goal: helping viewers understand how to confirm that the audio is usable before filming begins. This scenario is simply an illustrative example.

When dividing responsibilities, also identify which background information should be introduced only once and which terms should be explained consistently. If both speakers begin with a full account of their own background material, the audience may have to hear the same starting point twice. The opening can establish the overall scope, allowing subsequent speakers to move directly to the questions they are responsible for addressing. Speaking time does not need to be divided equally; it should reflect how much explanation each section requires.
body.heading2: Make the Connection Between Sections Clear in the Handoff
body.section2:
“I will now hand over to my partner” signals a change of speaker, but the transition can be more specific. For example: “We have now chosen our recording location. Next, please show us how to determine whether this audio clip is usable.” The audience understands both the purpose of the next section and how it relates to what came before.

I recommend that partners review their transition phrases together to check for any tasks they have not agreed on. Do not unexpectedly ask the other person to explain an example they have not prepared, or put them under pressure with an exaggerated introduction. If names, titles, or responsibilities are mentioned, confirm the correct wording beforehand. A clear introduction to the material the other person will cover is enough.

Pick Up Where the Previous Section Leaves Off

The incoming speaker can begin by building on the conclusion just reached before moving into new material. Continuing the earlier example, they might say: “Now that we have chosen the location, let us listen to a short test recording and check whether the voice is clear.” This keeps the explanation moving more effectively than introducing the entire filming project again. Adapt the sample wording to your natural speaking style rather than memorizing it as a fixed script.

If you need to add information your partner has left out, first consider whether it affects understanding. If it is simply an extra detail, save it for an agreed point in the presentation. If it concerns the procedure currently being demonstrated, briefly explain why the addition is needed, then hand back to the other speaker. Additional comments during a joint presentation should help the audience make the judgment at hand, rather than turn every detail into an unplanned exchange.

Rehearse Eye Contact and Equipment Handoffs Too

After delivering the transition phrase, turn naturally toward your partner and pause to let them begin. If each speaker has a microphone, agree on who will stop speaking first and when the other will start. If you share equipment, practice passing it during the sound check and make sure the audience can clearly hear the first sentence after the handoff. For an online joint presentation, also confirm in advance who controls the on-screen display, who advances the slides, and who continues if a connection drops.

If both speakers start talking at once, let the designated lead speaker finish a sentence before the other adds a comment. If the speaking order needs to change unexpectedly, briefly explain the change to the audience. Agree on reminder cues beforehand as well, such as a hand gesture both speakers can see, rather than repeatedly trying to interpret each other through eye contact during the presentation.

Rehearse the Transitions Separately Before Putting Everything Together

I recommend starting with a four-minute exercise: spend one minute confirming the conclusion of the previous section and the question addressed in the next, two minutes practicing the handoff and switching roles, and one minute reviewing the recording. This timing is simply an example of a rehearsal plan, not a standard for assessing ability. Focus on whether the incoming speaker repeats the introduction, whether the speakers talk over each other, and whether the audience can follow the connection between sections.

In creator education at PT. Otto Media Grup, public speaking and content production are closely connected. Joint livestreams, course demonstrations, and brand proposals may all require collaboration among several people. Building handoffs into the content plan and running through the presentation before recording can help teams identify gaps in responsibilities. This preparation also applies to collaborative presentations in Media Tech projects.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Giving Each Person Half the Speaking Time the Fairest Approach?

Time can be allocated according to the tasks involved. First, make sure each section can be explained clearly, then discuss how to arrange speaking time for both presenters. There is no need to split a complete explanation simply to achieve an equal division.

What If My Partner Covers My Main Points Before My Turn?

Build on what has already been explained, then add new examples, conditions, or procedures. There is no need to repeat the entire section during the presentation. Adjust the division of responsibilities afterward.

Do We Need to Write Out Every Transition Word for Word?

Start by writing down the key message, then rehearse it in language that feels natural to each of you. Where important names, figures, or procedural sequences are involved, preserve the precise wording.

Who Should Answer Questions During the Q&A?

Agree in advance on one person to confirm the question, then direct it to the appropriate speaker according to the topic. If the other person needs to add something, they should wait until the current answer is finished.

Closing Thoughts

The next time you present with a partner, I recommend starting your rehearsal at each point where the speaker changes. Give the previous section a clear conclusion, give the next section a specific purpose, and coordinate speech, eye contact, and equipment handoffs. This makes it easier for both presenters to guide the audience through one clear line of explanation.

title: Correcting Inaccurate Information During a Speech: How to Be Clear and Continue
summary: Author: Fandi Hasib When you realize during a speech that you have given inaccurate information, I recommend first stopping the incorrect explanation, identifying the specific point that needs correcting, and then…

body.intro:
Author: Fandi Hasib

When you realize during a speech that you have given inaccurate information, I recommend first stopping the incorrect explanation, identifying the specific point that needs correcting, and then clearly stating the verified version and its implications. If the correct answer is still uncertain, explicitly leave the matter unresolved and hold off on any conclusions that depend on it. This article distinguishes between slips of the tongue, factual errors, and information awaiting verification, helping speakers explain corrections clearly in the moment while also considering recordings and supporting materials.

Journalism and public speaking both require careful attention to accuracy. My name is Fandi Hasib. I have worked in Indonesia as a journalist, television news anchor, and program producer, alongside public speaking training and BIPA, or Indonesian language education for foreign speakers. I participate in the creator education program at PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content production, and I also teach public speaking classes open to the public through opportunities provided by the company. Across these communication settings, I recommend making correction skills part of regular rehearsal.
body.heading1: First, Determine Whether the Error Changed the Meaning
body.section1:
If you briefly stumble over pronunciation without changing the meaning, say the word clearly and continue. If you give an incorrect date, name, organization, or scope of application, however, the audience needs to know exactly what has changed. Simply saying, “There was a small issue just now,” is not enough, because listeners will not know which note to revise.

Another possibility is that you suddenly realize you are unsure. In that situation, avoid substituting another answer based on instinct. You can say directly, “I need to check this point again, so I will not use it as a basis for a conclusion yet.” Whether you can move on to the next section depends on whether it relies on that information. If it does, pause the related line of reasoning.
body.heading2: Make the Correction Clear Enough to Stand on Its Own
body.section2:
I recommend using complete sentences to identify what you are correcting and state the correct version. Suppose an event in a practice scenario is actually scheduled for Friday, but the speaker mistakenly says Thursday. The correction could be: “A correction: the event I just mentioned is scheduled for Friday. Please plan for Friday.” This example is for practice only and does not refer to an actual event.

If the change affects what listeners need to do next, explain that impact as well. For example, when correcting a registration deadline in a demonstration, restate when submissions must be made rather than merely giving a new date. After the correction, allow a brief pause for listeners to update their notes, then resume with a complete thought.

An apology should be proportionate to the impact of the error. When important information has misled the audience, clearly taking responsibility and providing a correction is more useful than a lengthy explanation of why you were nervous. If the error concerns the name of another person or facts about them, check carefully and avoid using humor to minimize the mistake.

When an Audience Member Flags an Issue, Verify Before Responding

When someone points out a problem, first listen fully to identify the statement they mean, then check whether you are both referring to the same time, subject, or version. If you did make an error, correct it directly. If you cannot yet determine whether the information is wrong, explain that you need to consult the materials. Thanking someone for raising a concern does not mean accepting a new claim without verification.

Two questions can help organize your thinking at this point: “What specific information do we disagree on?” and “What reliable materials are available here to check it?” If there is insufficient evidence on hand, leave the issue open. Commit to a time and method for replying only when you are certain you can complete the follow-up verification. Avoid making promises you cannot keep simply to bring the exchange to a quick end.

Carry the Correction Through to Recordings and Supporting Materials

After making the correction clearly during the session, consider how the content may be viewed again. In course recordings, livestream replays, or short videos, viewers may see only the earlier segment containing the error. I recommend locating the error and, depending on the publication format, adding a clear correction notice to the relevant segment or updating the description and supporting materials so that later viewers can find the accurate version.

This is also where public speaking connects with content production. Creator education at PT. Otto Media Grup covers both fields. In Media Tech, digital marketing, and collaborations between brands and creators, live presentations may also become content that continues to circulate. Corrections should account for audiences watching different versions; do not assume that everyone heard the final clarification.

Use a Short Rehearsal to Practice the Pace of a Correction

Choose a practice script that has already been checked for accuracy. Speak normally for one minute, then introduce a clearly marked slip-of-the-tongue scenario, spend about twenty seconds delivering the correction, and finally repeat the complete passage. This is a self-directed practice arrangement. Twenty seconds is not a time limit for handling errors during a live session, nor should it be used to rush through complex disputes.

When listening back, check whether the correction can be understood without the surrounding context: Is the subject clear? Is the correct information clear? Have the implications been explained? A practice partner who hears only the correction should still know what information to retain. If anything is missing, add it and practice again rather than simply trying to speak faster.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I Still Need to Correct an Error If the Audience Does Not Seem to Have Noticed?

If the error affects facts, meaning, or actions, it should be corrected. The absence of objections from the audience does not mean the error had no impact.

What If It Is Only a Pronunciation Slip That Does Not Affect Understanding?

Simply repeat the word clearly. There is no need to turn a minor pause into a lengthy explanation. Take particular care to verify key information such as names.

What If I Cannot Find the Correct Information During the Session?

Explain which information remains unverified and hold off on conclusions that depend on it. Provide the accurate findings afterward through a follow-up method you can reliably carry out, rather than replacing the error with another guess.

Is It Enough to Remove the Incorrect Segment from the Replay?

You should also check whether the remaining content is complete and whether people who saw the incorrect version can learn about the correction. Important changes can be clearly marked in the description or related materials.

Closing Thoughts

I recommend including a correction exercise in your next speech rehearsal. When you discover a problem, give the audience a clear, verifiable correction, then continue with the content that remains valid. Accuracy should be maintained throughout both the live presentation and its subsequent distribution.

title: When No One Answers: How to Encourage an Audience to Speak Up
summary: Author: Fandi Hasib When no one responds to a question during a session, I recommend first allowing time to think, then narrowing the question to a specific choice and explaining how the audience can participate. If the…

body.intro:
Author: Fandi Hasib

When no one responds to a question during a session, I recommend first allowing time to think, then narrowing the question to a specific choice and explaining how the audience can participate. If the room remains quiet, offer a practice example and move naturally to the next section. This article discusses interaction in public classes, talks, and livestreams, focusing on making it easier for audiences to respond while preserving the option not to speak.

My work spans journalism and language teaching. I am Fandi Hasib, and I have worked in Indonesia as a journalist, television news anchor, and producer, as well as in public speaking training and BIPA, or Indonesian language teaching for foreign speakers. Within the creator education program at PT. Otto Media Grup, I focus on public speaking and content production, and the company also provides opportunities for me to teach public speaking courses to the public. When designing audience interaction, I recommend starting with whether listeners can understand the question and answer it comfortably.
body.heading1: First, Check Whether the Question Is Easy to Answer
body.section1:
“What does everyone think?” leaves the scope of the answer up to the audience. They first have to decide what to discuss, then put their thoughts into words. When preparing a talk, I recommend making questions more specific. For example, after introducing the process of preparing for a livestream, you could ask, “Which would you like to learn about first: checking the audio or outlining the content?” This gives the audience a clear starting point and helps the speaker understand how the response will connect to what follows.

Questions that offer a choice should still leave room for other answers. If neither option fits, allow listeners to describe another possibility. When a topic involves personal difficulties, income, or mistakes at work, there is no need to require public sharing. Anonymous submissions or analysis of a fictional scenario give participants more options. The following question revisions are practice examples, not records of actual classroom exchanges.
body.heading2: Avoid Adding More Questions While You Wait
body.section2:
After asking a question, I recommend pausing and looking calmly around the audience. If you immediately add two more questions, listeners have to decide again which one to answer. During rehearsal, try leaving five seconds of silence and notice whether you feel an urge to fill the gap. Five seconds is only a starting point for practice, not a standard that should apply to every live setting.

If a question requires listeners to recall an experience or read some material, explicitly say, “Take a moment to think,” or “Write down one keyword first.” For complex questions, you can also give the audience time to think independently before inviting voluntary responses. Do not automatically interpret silence as a sign that listeners are inattentive, uninterested, or already understand the material. Silence alone does not support any of those conclusions.

Explain How to Participate, Then Acknowledge the First Response

Speaking publicly is only one way to participate. Listeners can also raise their hands to indicate a choice, write down keywords, or submit questions through the chat. The speaker should explain in advance which method will be used and how the feedback will be used afterward. If someone answers, “I am concerned about the audio,” first restate that concern, then move into the relevant explanation. Avoid changing the subject as soon as someone starts contributing.

Sometimes, no one responds even then. I recommend preparing a fallback prompt, such as, “Let me illustrate this with a hypothetical scenario: if the picture is clear but the sound keeps getting louder and quieter, what should we check next?” This provides material for discussion without guessing what the audience thinks. Make it clear that the fallback example is hypothetical, and do not present your prepared answer as a consensus reached in the room.

Use a Short Rehearsal to Find What You Can Improve

Try a four-minute practice round: spend one minute writing the original question, one minute narrowing its scope, one minute practicing the pause and transition, and the final minute reviewing an audio or video recording. Check just one thing in each round, such as whether you asked three questions in succession while waiting. These timings and repetitions are intended for individual practice, not as statistical findings about the effectiveness of audience interaction.

In creator education and content production settings associated with PT. Otto Media Grup, this exercise can also be used for livestream scripts. Including questions, pauses, and transitions after responses in the running order makes them easier to carry out live. After the livestream, review which questions generated feedback that could support further discussion. For Media Tech content, it is worth looking beyond the number of comments to consider whether the feedback helped viewers understand the topic.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I Call on Someone Directly?

In a class where participation rules have been agreed in advance, follow those arrangements. With an unfamiliar audience or at an open event, prioritize voluntary responses and allow people to pass.

What If Online Viewers Keep Leaving No Comments?

First, confirm that the comment feature is working, then check whether the question is specific and the participation instructions are clear. After giving an example, you can continue the explanation without repeatedly prompting viewers to respond.

How Do I Bring an Off-Topic Answer Back to the Subject?

First, acknowledge the point the person is focused on, then explain the question this section is intended to address. Discussion that is valuable but outside the scope can be saved for an appropriate question-and-answer session.

Should I Include Interaction Every Few Minutes?

There is no fixed interval. Ask questions when you need to understand audience preferences, check understanding, or invite practice. Avoid interrupting a complete explanation merely to make the session livelier.

Closing Thoughts

The next time you prepare a talk, I recommend choosing the most important interaction question and writing out its specific wording, the method of participation, and the transition to use if no one responds. Make it clear how listeners can join the discussion, while ensuring that you can continue the explanation with confidence.

title: Make Your Slides Support Your Talk, Not Run It
summary: How can you deliver a prepared slide deck naturally without missing the key points? Give each slide a clear explanatory purpose: first tell the audience what to look at, then explain how it relates to your topic, and…

body.intro:
How can you deliver a prepared slide deck naturally without missing the key points? Give each slide a clear explanatory purpose: first tell the audience what to look at, then explain how it relates to your topic, and finally bring their attention back to the conversation. This article explores slide selection, transitions, and rehearsal to help people delivering classes, proposals, or online presentations make their visuals and spoken explanations complement each other.

This challenge draws on several areas of the professional background of Fandi Hasib: news reporting in Indonesia, television news presenting and production, public speaking training, and BIPA, or Indonesian language teaching for non-native speakers.
