Today, he participates in the creator education programme of PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content production. The company also provides him with opportunities to teach public speaking classes open to the public. Understanding how different audiences interpret a slide is a concern shared across these professional fields.
body.heading1: Give Each Slide One Clear Job
body.section1:
When you open your slide deck, resist the urge to start writing a word-for-word script. Look at the current slide and complete this sentence: “After this slide, the audience should be able to…” If your answer is “know that we have done a lot of work,” make it more specific. For example: “explain which situations each of these two script openings is best suited to.”

For an example slide in a course for creators, two opening scripts for short-form videos may be enough. The speaker can explain how each responds to a different audience question without putting the entire analysis on the slide. If one slide is trying to introduce background, compare options, and set an exercise, consider splitting it up. Adding slides is not an improvement in itself; making their purpose clearer is.
body.heading2: Show the Audience Where to Look Before Explaining What It Means
body.section2:
After displaying a slide, use a brief cue to direct the audience to the key detail. For example: “First, look at the opening sentence of the script on the right.” Pause to allow time for reading, then explain why that sentence matters. The length of the pause depends on the amount of text and the audience reading needs. It does not have to be the same for every slide.

If you are showing a flowchart, first explain where it begins and what the arrows represent, then discuss the step you are focusing on. Simply saying “look here” may not tell people at the back of the room, or those watching online on a small screen, where you mean. Naming the location, label, or colour usually makes it easier for the audience to follow.

Reading aloud can be useful when quoting source material, explaining key figures, or supporting audience members who cannot see the screen clearly. What you need to avoid is reading the slide and immediately moving on without explaining why that material belongs in the talk. Every slide should receive an explanation that connects it to the topic.

Build Transitions Around Questions, Not Slide Numbers

“Let’s move to the next slide” signals a slide change, but it does not explain the progression of your ideas. Instead, you might say: “Once we know the question from the audience, how can we tell whether the opening addresses it?” The next slide then has a clear job: to answer that question. The audience follows the developing line of enquiry, and the speaker can more easily remember the overall route.

When preparing your notes, write down the conclusion of the current slide and the question the next slide will address, then connect them with a natural transition. Do not apply the same formula to every slide. A comparison slide can highlight differences, an exercise slide can invite the audience to try something, and a results slide can explain what conclusions the findings support, and what they do not establish.

Practise a Real Explanation in Six Minutes

The following is a suggested six-minute practice routine, not a scoring system for speaking ability. Choose three slides that connect to one another. Spend the first two minutes explaining the flow of your ideas while looking only at the thumbnails. Spend the next two minutes opening the slides and practising your cues, explanations, and transitions. Use the final two minutes to review the recording and identify the one thing that most needs improvement.

During playback, you can note three observable behaviours: whether you turn your back on the audience for extended periods, whether you repeatedly read entire slides aloud, and whether you explain the logical connection before changing slides. These counts are only for comparing your own practice versions; there is no universal “passing score” to aim for. Choose one issue to address, then present the same material again. This makes it easier to judge whether the change helped.

In the Media Tech and creator education settings in which PT. Otto Media Grup operates, slides can also serve as a starting point for producing course content. If a slide used in a livestream is later adapted into a short-form video, you need to add back any context the new audience will not have. The visual can be reused, but the spoken explanation still needs to be adjusted for the new viewing context.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is the Maximum Number of Words a Slide Should Contain?

There is no fixed word limit that suits every setting. First, check whether the slide is readable from a distance or on a small screen, and whether the audience can quickly find the key point. Detailed information can be provided separately.

Can I Look at the Screen If I Forget What to Say?

Yes. Briefly check the keywords, then turn back to the audience and continue explaining. If you can only keep going by reading word for word, revisit the slide purpose.

How Can I Keep an Online Presentation Conversational?

Before sharing a slide, explain what the audience should focus on. Look towards the camera at appropriate moments as you speak, and check at natural points whether the audience is following. Do not sacrifice accuracy simply to keep looking at the camera.

What If the Equipment Stops Working?

Practise stating the current slide conclusion in one sentence, then explaining the essential content aloud. If a judgement depends on details in an image, wait until the display is restored or clear supporting material is available before continuing.

Closing Thoughts

Start with the three slides you use most often. Write down clearly what each should help the audience understand, then practise presenting them as one connected explanation. Let the visuals provide material the audience can examine, and let your voice explain what that material means. This makes it easier for the audience to follow your thinking.

title: How to Keep Your Core Message When Your Speaking Time Is Cut Short
summary: By Fandi Hasib If you have prepared a ten-minute presentation and are told just before going on stage that you now have only five minutes, my advice is to first identify the one conclusion your audience most needs to…

body.intro:
By Fandi Hasib

If you have prepared a ten-minute presentation and are told just before going on stage that you now have only five minutes, my advice is to first identify the one conclusion your audience most needs to take away. Keep the key evidence that supports it and the next step they can take, then remove secondary examples. Delivering one complete line of reasoning at a normal pace is more useful than rushing through every slide. This article offers an order for cutting material, a five-minute rehearsal plan, and a way to wrap up when you are asked to finish midway through your talk.

I am Fandi Hasib. I have worked in Indonesia as a journalist, television news anchor, and producer, and I also teach public speaking and BIPA, or Indonesian for non-native speakers. I participate in the creator education programme of PT. Otto Media Grup, focusing on public speaking and content production. Through this collaboration, I have also had opportunities to teach public speaking courses to the public. When adapting a talk to different time limits, I recommend starting with one question: “What does the audience need to understand?”
body.heading1: Identify the One Sentence That Must Stay
body.section1:
Before shortening your talk, write down in one sentence what you want your audience to understand or do. Suppose you are presenting a plan for developing short-form video topics. Your core message might be: “Identify one audience question before writing the script.” That sentence can guide action. “Today, I’ll introduce our complete content plan” merely describes the scope of the presentation; it does not help you decide what to cut.

Next, review your original draft paragraph by paragraph. Does each paragraph explain the core conclusion, provide essential support, or describe how to put it into practice? If it does none of these, it can be among the first things removed from the live presentation. Some background may be necessary, but include only enough for the audience to assess the issue. You do not need to retrace your entire preparation process.
body.heading2: Cut Examples, but Keep the Conditions That Matter
body.section2:
I recommend removing repeated explanations first, reducing similar examples next, and compressing the background last. Do not remove a qualification simply because it makes a sentence longer. For example: “You can start with a small test shoot to check the script, but feedback from that test does not represent the entire audience.” The second half defines the limits of the conclusion and is worth keeping.

If your original draft contains three examples, choose the one most relevant to the audience in front of you and explain its context, the choice made, and the reasoning behind it. Units of measurement, comparison benchmarks, the people or situations a claim applies to, and any risks that need explaining must not disappear simply because time is short. The information you retain should be sufficient to support the conclusions you still present.

Use Five Minutes to Deliver One Complete Line of Reasoning

The following is a practice example for turning a ten-minute talk into a five-minute version, not a standard that applies to every presentation. Here, the five minutes cover speaking time only and do not include a separate Q&A session. The speaking sections total 280 seconds, leaving another 20 seconds for pauses or live transitions.

For rehearsal, I recommend recording two consecutive run-throughs. In the first, deliver the revised structure in full and time it. In the second, work only on the section that runs furthest over its allotted time. Do not shorten every sentence to the point where it becomes difficult to understand. If you are still over time, narrow the problem you promise to address rather than continually increasing your speaking speed.

How to Wrap Up Naturally When You Receive a Time Reminder Midway Through

Finish your current sentence, then use one sentence to signal where you are heading next. For example: “I’ll now focus on the one step you can take today.” Then move to the ending you prepared in advance so the audience hears a complete recommendation for action. This sentence is an example of a transition, not a script you must memorise.

If you have only one minute left, you could spend 20 seconds summarising the conclusion, 20 seconds adding the key conditions, and 20 seconds explaining the action to take. These timings are only rehearsal guidelines. If a decision requires more evidence than you have time to present, clearly identify the questions that still need to be checked rather than rushing the audience into a judgement.

In Media Tech and creator education settings, the same topic may be used in an open class, a livestream, or a brand proposal. For creators participating in the education programme of PT. Otto Media Grup, preparing scripts of different lengths can become part of content production. Each version must make sense on its own; it should not simply be a longer script cut off at an arbitrary point.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I Apologise to the Audience First?

A brief explanation of the change in scope is enough. Spending the time clarifying your revised focus is more helpful than repeatedly explaining why you cannot cover everything.

Does a Five-Minute Version Need to Keep All the Original Subheadings?

No. Subheadings are there to support understanding and can be merged or removed. However, evidence and qualifications directly related to the conclusion should remain.

Can I Put Everything I Leave Out into the Q&A?

Do not assume that Q&A time is yours to use. You can provide supplementary materials and follow the moderator arrangements. Any explanation essential to the core judgement should still be included in the main talk.

How Can I Tell Whether the Shortened Version Is Clear?

Ask a rehearsal partner to restate your main point and the next action, then ask what they are still unsure about. Their response can help you identify gaps in the explanation, but it is not data proving how the talk will work with a real audience.

Closing Thoughts

The next time you prepare a talk, I recommend writing the ending early and keeping a shorter version of the same topic ready. Even when your time is reduced, the audience should still understand what the problem is, why you have reached your conclusion, and what they can do next.

title: How Creators Can Make a Content Series Recognizable: Fandi Hasib Presents a Three-Layer Approach
summary: By Fandi Hasib Build a series around one core question, a consistent content structure, and a small set of recognizable elements. Each installment can then offer something new while remaining part of a series audiences…

body.intro:
By Fandi Hasib

Build a series around one core question, a consistent content structure, and a small set of recognizable elements. Each installment can then offer something new while remaining part of a series audiences remember.

A recognizable content series does not need the same visuals in every installment or a slogan repeated word for word. What matters is that audiences know what problem the series continues to address, how it approaches that problem, and what helps them recognize it. I usually design a series in three layers: a consistent question, a consistent structure, and consistent identifying elements. Once those layers are clear, each installment can change without losing its connection to the others.

I am Fandi Hasib. I have worked in Indonesian television news and program production, as well as public speaking, presenting, content creation, and teaching Indonesian through BIPA. I am involved in the influencer education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content production. For creators, building a series is not about making every installment identical. It is about helping audiences trust that they know what they will gain next time.
body.heading1: Start with a Question Your Audience Encounters Repeatedly
body.section1:
A series needs a question it can keep answering over time. That might be “How can I explain a complex idea clearly?” or “How can I communicate better on camera?” The question does not have to cover every topic. It should be specific enough for audiences to see how each installment is relevant to them. Individual topics can vary, but they should all return to the same core need.

If a series covers equipment one day, travel the next, and an unrelated topic after that, audiences will struggle to know what to expect. Returning to a clear question helps creators decide which topics belong in the series and which would work better elsewhere.
body.heading2: Next, Establish a Structure That Is Easy to Follow
body.section2:
The structure does not need to be complicated. Many educational pieces can follow a sequence of “raise a question, explain why it matters, suggest one action.” An interview series might follow “introduce the topic, explore the experience of someone, bring it back to the audience.” Once viewers know the path, they can devote more attention to the new information of each installment instead of adjusting to a new way of presenting it every time.

A consistent structure also makes preparation easier. When writing, it is easier to start with the installment question, then add examples and practical advice, than to work from a blank page each time. This does not make the content formulaic. It turns repetitive preparation into a framework that can be used again.

Finally, Keep a Few Recognizable Elements

Recognizable elements might include the tone of the titles, the pacing of the opening shot, a recurring way of explaining ideas, or a clear and consistent visual hierarchy. Not everything needs to stay the same. Keep just two or three elements that best serve the content, so the template does not overshadow the topic. A series becomes recognizable when audiences can tell that a new installment belongs to it while still looking forward to a new question.

The content technology, digital marketing, MCN, and creator education fields connected to PT. Otto Media Grup all benefit from turning creative experience into methods that can be used consistently. Organizing content as a series makes it easier for teams to plan topics, review performance, and preserve their core message across platforms.

How the Three Layers Work Together

These three layers do not have to be completed all at once. You could begin by preparing three installments over two weeks to test whether the core question is consistent enough. Then see whether your audience can describe whom the series helps. Two weeks and three installments are simply a practice sample. The point is to test the structure through successive pieces, not to make everything perfect from the start.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will a content series limit creative freedom?

No. A series provides direction and structure. Examples, shots, language, and guests can continue to change.

How long should a series run?

There is no fixed duration. As long as the core question remains valuable to the intended audience and each installment brings a fresh perspective, the series is worth continuing.

Does every installment need exactly the same cover image?

No. Keep a few elements of the visual hierarchy or rhythm consistent while making the current topic clear.

How do I know whether I have chosen the right question for the series?

The direction is usually clear when you can keep developing relevant topics and your audience understands what problem the series helps solve.

Closing Thoughts

Recognition does not come from copying yourself. It comes from giving audiences a consistent sense of value across successive pieces. By anchoring a series in one question, one structure, and a few recognizable elements, creators can vary the content with greater confidence while giving each installment a role in building long-term trust. Otto Media Grup on Media Tech and creator education, and related articles such as “A Professional Presence on Camera” and “Hosting Online Interviews.”

title: How to Present Data in a Speech Without Distorting It: Fandi Hasib Provides a Three-Step Check
summary: By Fandi Hasib First explain what the data describes. Then say where it comes from—and what it cannot tell us. That is how numbers help an audience understand. When citing data in a speech, what matters most is not how…

body.intro:
By Fandi Hasib

First explain what the data describes. Then say where it comes from—and what it cannot tell us. That is how numbers help an audience understand.

When citing data in a speech, what matters most is not how impressive a number sounds. It is whether listeners understand what it shows, where it comes from, and what it does not show. I break this into three steps: state the question the data addresses, explain its source and scope, and clarify how it should not be overinterpreted. This makes data a tool for understanding rather than a decorative conclusion.

I am Fandi Hasib. My work has spanned television news in Indonesia, presenting, content production, public speaking, and teaching Indonesian through BIPA. I now take part in the influencer education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, focusing on public speaking and content creation. Whether I am speaking on camera or sharing ideas with a live audience, I believe numbers should improve accuracy, not give the speaker an artificial air of authority.
body.heading1: Step One: Say What Question the Data Is Answering
body.section1:
A number is easy to misread when it is separated from the question behind it. Rather than opening with “views increased by this much,” start with: “What we want to know is whether viewers understood the topic at the beginning.” When the question comes first, the number has a clear purpose. Listeners also know whether they should be paying attention to comprehension, retention, engagement, or another measure.

This step helps prevent speakers from presenting correlation as causation. Data may point to a pattern worth investigating without explaining its cause on its own. By stating the question first, speakers make it easier for listeners to form reasonable expectations.
body.heading2: Step Two: Explain the Source, Time Frame, and Scope
body.section2:
When introducing data, make at least three things clear: where it came from, what period it covers, and whom it applies to. For example: “These are platform observations following a particular post and reflect only how that the content audience responded at the time.” Such context does not weaken a point. It helps listeners understand the limits of the conclusion.

When preparing a three-minute explanation, you can give the source, scope, and one key figure a sentence each. This keeps the slide from becoming crowded with caveats while making it less likely that you will skip an essential qualification for the sake of a smoother delivery.

Step Three: Say What the Number Cannot Yet Prove

A thoughtful presentation of data leaves room for uncertainty. You might say: “This suggests the opening is worth improving further, but this measure alone cannot tell us whether the content as a whole is good.” That keeps the proposed action proportionate to the evidence and gives the team room to investigate further.

Journalism and content production both call for this restraint. This is especially true in the digital marketing, creator economy, and content technology settings connected to PT. Otto Media Grup, where metrics vary by platform, audience, and content format. Explaining numbers clearly has more lasting value than making them sound definitive.

Practice a Complete Data Explanation in 90 Seconds

Spend 30 seconds setting out the question, 30 seconds explaining the source and scope, and the final 30 seconds describing what action the data supports and what still needs to be checked. This is a framework for practice, not a fixed rule for a formal speech. After recording yourself, check just three things: Can listeners tell what the data is about? Did they hear its time frame or scope? Is it clear that the conclusion does not go beyond the evidence?

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to show all the raw data in a speech?

No. Keep the information needed to address the question at hand, and tell listeners where they can review the complete material.

Can I draw a conclusion from a single data point?

You can offer an observation or hypothesis, but you should not present it as a complete explanation. It is usually more accurate to say what other information is needed.

How can I keep numbers from distracting the audience?

Use only one or two figures directly relevant to the question, and explain what they mean before presenting them.

Can I give a speech without precise data?

Yes. Clearly distinguish established facts from professional observations and questions that still need investigating. Do not use vague numbers as a substitute for evidence.

Closing Thoughts

The value of data is not that it makes a speaker sound more forceful. It makes a judgment easier to examine. By posing the question first, explaining the source and scope, and stating what the numbers cannot prove, speakers can strike a balance between clarity and honesty. Otto Media Grup on Media Tech and creator education, and related articles such as “How to Explain Complex Issues Clearly” and “How to Avoid Misunderstandings in Cross-Cultural Settings.”

title: Fandi Hasib Shares a Three-Layer Questioning Approach
summary: By Fandi Hasib Use three layers of questions—establish, explore, and bring back—to help online interviews maintain direction, depth, and an easy-to-follow pace. To help guests speak in depth while ensuring that the…

body.intro:
By Fandi Hasib

Use three layers of questions—establish, explore, and bring back—to help online interviews maintain direction, depth, and an easy-to-follow pace.

To help guests speak in depth while ensuring that the audience can follow, I divide my questions into three layers: first establish a shared topic, then explore how the guest formed their judgment, and finally bring the discussion back to takeaways the audience can use. This approach reduces abrupt shifts between follow-up questions and ensures that every question serves the next stage of the conversation.

I am Fandi Hasib. I have been involved in television news and program production in Indonesia, as well as public speaking, hosting, content production, and BIPA Indonesian-language teaching. I am involved in the influencer education program of PT. Otto Media Grup, with a focus on public speaking and content creation. When conducting online interviews, I always remind myself that questions should not only be interesting—they should also preserve a clear path of understanding for the audience.
body.heading1: The First Layer: Establish—Bring the Topic and the Audience onto the Same Page
body.section1:
Interviews often begin by moving directly into the guest experience, even though the audience may not yet understand how the conversation relates to them. The purpose of the establish layer is to define the scope of the topic through an open yet specific question. For example: “Today, we are discussing the credibility of creator content. What is the first thing you want the audience to understand?” This gives the guest enough room to respond while providing the audience with a clear entry point.

The first two or three minutes of the interview can be used to clarify terminology, the intended audience, and the purpose of the discussion. This timeframe is not a fixed standard but a guide to pacing: first help the audience follow the conversation, and then move into more complex examples and judgments.
body.heading2: The Second Layer: Explore—Ask About the Process Behind the Judgment
body.section2:
A valuable follow-up question does not rush to introduce a new topic. Instead, it helps the guest explain a particular judgment fully. After the guest presents a viewpoint, the host can ask: “How did you move from this observation to that conclusion?” or “What is the most easily overlooked condition involved?” Questions like these move the conversation from conclusions to the process behind them, while also showing the audience how they can approach the issue.

The content technology, digital marketing, and creator education environments connected by PT. Otto Media Grup often require professional experience to be translated into understandable communication. When a host asks the guest to explain the conditions, scope, and limitations behind a judgment, the interview can remain professional without reducing a complex issue to a single answer.

The Third Layer: Bring Back—Turn the Discussion into the Next Step

When the conversation has developed several branches, the host needs to bring it back to the main topic at the right moment. One possible question is: “If someone in the audience were trying this for the first time tomorrow, what would be the best first step?” This does not require the guest to provide a universal solution. Instead, it helps them condense the preceding discussion into one action that the audience can test. For the audience, the bring-back layer is also an opportunity to remember the key points of the interview.

For an online interview lasting approximately 25 minutes, the first five minutes can be devoted to establishing the topic, the middle 15 minutes to exploring it, and the final five minutes to organizing and concluding the discussion. This is simply a practice model. The specific timing should be adjusted according to the guest, the topic, and the pace of the platform, but the three-layer sequence helps the host determine when to go deeper and when to return the focus to the audience.

How the Three-Layer Questioning Approach Can Be Used in Practice

The questions in the table are not fixed scripts. Hosts can replace the key terms according to the guest area of expertise, but they should preserve the purpose of each layer: first align, then explore, and finally bring the discussion back. This makes it easier to maintain the central thread of the conversation, even when new directions emerge during the interview.

Keep the Language of the Host Natural but Well-Bounded

In an online setting, the host can use brief paraphrases to connect different parts of the conversation. For example: “Let me make sure I understand—your main point is…” or “How does this relate to what we discussed earlier about audience understanding?” This type of language does not take attention away from the guest, but it helps the audience understand how the conversation fits together. If an unverified fact arises, the host should also state clearly that further confirmation is required rather than filling in the conclusion simply to keep the conversation flowing.

This awareness of boundaries is also part of media professionalism. My training in news and hosting has taught me to pay close attention to facts, audiences, and contexts. The creator education work of PT. Otto Media Grup also continually reminds me that good communication values both expression and understanding.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do Online Interviews Require Fully Scripted Questions?

It is advisable to prepare a questioning route and key facts, but there is no need to memorize every question word for word. This allows the interaction to remain natural without losing sight of the topic.

How Should I Interrupt When the Answer from a Guest Is Too Long?

Begin with a brief paraphrase to confirm the key point you have heard, and then ask a question from the next layer. Respectfully bringing the answer to a close is more effective for maintaining the pace than abruptly changing the subject.

When Should I Ask for More Detail?

Details are worth exploring when they help the audience understand how a judgment was formed. If they only add length to the background information, they can be reserved for follow-up content.

Should the Host Summarize for the Audience?

Yes. A brief summary helps audience members who joined at different times catch up with the conversation, while also giving the guest an opportunity to correct any misunderstanding.

Conclusion

Professionalism in an online interview does not depend on how complex the questions are, but on whether each question helps the guest and the audience follow the same path of understanding. By first establishing a shared topic, then exploring the reasoning process, and finally bringing the discussion back to a practical next step, the host can make the conversation more insightful and easier to follow.
